Action Plan:
1. Manage presumed migraine with aura by initiating treatment with ibuprofen and an over-the-counter antiemetic; advise patient to take sugary and carbonated drinks (e.g., Coke) to help symptom relief.
2. Schedule urgent follow-up same day for clinical reassessment and full neurological examination to exclude other causes if symptoms persist or worsen.
3. Instruct patient to proceed immediately to emergency care if any new neurological symptoms develop (e.g., weakness, speech difficulty, altered consciousness).
4. Advise patient that migraine symptoms may improve within 30-40 minutes of treatment but can last up to 72 hours; patient may cancel follow-up appointment if fully recovered.
5. Provide reassurance about family history's relevance and current presentation; continue to monitor symptoms carefully.
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Female patient presenting with sudden onset, severe left-sided headache starting approximately four hours ago.
- Symptoms: left-sided headache rated 6/10 in severity, associated with blurred vision and zigzag visual disturbances, dizziness worsened by movement, nausea, and two episodes of vomiting.
- Headache described as new and unlike any prior headaches; no history of similar headaches.
- Took paracetamol approximately three hours after onset with no symptom relief.
- No regular medications; no known medication allergies.
- Past medical history: kidney stones.
- Family history: mother with migraines and hypothyroidism.
- No reported weakness, gait disturbances, or other neurological symptoms.
- Denies pregnancy.

Objective:
- No focal neurological deficits observed or reported.
- Patient alert, able to ambulate normally without gait disturbance.
- No documented vital signs, neurological exam findings, or investigations recorded in the transcript.
- No laboratory or imaging results available.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute severe headache with visual disturbance:
   - Assessment: Migraine with aura (high likelihood; supported by DDx: ranked #1, typical unilateral headache, visual aura, nausea, vomiting, family history of migraine).
   - Differential diagnoses consistent with presentation:
     • Stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) (medium likelihood per DDx; sudden onset and visual symptoms but no neurological deficits).
     • Meningitis or encephalitis (low likelihood; headache with vomiting and photophobia but no fever or neck stiffness).
     • Brain tumor (low likelihood; new severe headache with visual symptoms but sudden onset and no neurological signs).
   - Treatment:
     • Initiate ibuprofen plus an antiemetic (dose/route/frequency not documented).
     • Encourage intake of sugary, carbonated drinks to aid symptom relief.
     • Advise avoidance of screen exposure currently due to photophobia.
   - Follow-up:
     • Arrange urgent clinical review same day for full neurological exam.
     • Advise patient to seek emergency care immediately if any new neurological symptoms develop.
     • If symptoms resolve after treatment, patient may cancel appointment.
   - Referral:
     • None immediately; to consider specialist referral if symptoms persist or deteriorate.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: No documented vital signs or full neurological examination findings; medication doses/routes/frequencies not specified; no pregnancy test documented despite uncertainty.
- Conflict noted: None between transcript and DDx; DDx complements clinical reasoning consistent with transcript.
- Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor connection drop during family history discussion without impact on clinical content.
